newsitem.title: USA: Rights groups side with Oklahoma bomb victims.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups side with Oklahoma bomb victims.

text.p: Victims rights groups from around the United States Wednesday gave their support to Oklahoma City bombing survivors in their legal battle for access to court proceedings in the case.
Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols, former army buddies, are accused of the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, in which 168 people died.
McVeigh is to go on trial March 31 in Denver and Nichols at an undetermined later date. The trial was moved to Denver because of extensive publicity about the bombing in Oklahoma.

Groups including Justice for Surviving Victims and Mothers Against Drunk Driving joined victims and prosecutors in urging a federal appeals court to overturn part of a ban excluding victims from court sessions if they are to be witnesses in the upcoming trials.

U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch issued the ban this year, saying victims' testimony about the impact of the crime on their lives could be influenced if they attended the trial. But victims and prosecutors disagreed and argued that the ban should not apply to victims who would testify only in the sentencing phase of the trials if defendants are convicted.
The victims are not appealing the part of the ban that excludes them if they will testify in the guilt-innocence phase of the trials.

At least eight victims rights groups, also including the National Victim Centre and the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, a reform group, joined the Oklahoma City victims in arguing against Matsch's ban. The groups made their claims in "friend of the court" arguments to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver.
Prosecutors, on behalf of the victims, and the victims themselves were to file separate, written arguments.
Attorneys for Nichols and McVeigh, who support Matsch's ban, were to submit their arguments later.
